Life
LYFE
n. (animate existence, natural and spiritual; the vitality God alone possesses in Himself and gives to His creatures; rendering Hebrew chayyim, nephesh and Greek zōē, psychē, bios)
From Old English līf, common Germanic, related to to live and to leave in the sense of remaining. Hebrew chayyim is plural in form — lives — and takes singular agreement, a plural of abundance suggesting fullness rather than number. Greek distinguishes what English cannot: bios is the life one lives, its span and means (whence biography, biology); psychē is the animating soul-life a man may lose or save; zōē is life as principle and gift, the word John uses for what is in the Son.

Biblical Definition

Life belongs to God alone underivatively; every other life is loan and gift. Man receives it by a direct divine act: “the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul” (Gen 2:7). Because life is given, it is owed — which grounds the sixth commandment, the sanctity of the unborn, and the blood-prohibition of Gen 9. Natural life is real but brief and unpossessable: “What is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away” (Jas 4:14). Scripture then uses the word for a second and higher thing. Spiritual life is not the enhancement of natural life but its resurrection: men dead in trespasses and sins are quickened (Eph 2:1–5), and this life is located wholly in the Son — “In him was life; and the life was the light of men” (Joh 1:4). Christ came that His sheep “might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly” (Joh 10:10), a promise about the quality and permanence of the life given, not about circumstances. Eternal life begins now by faith, is preserved by the perseverance God works in His own, and is consummated in the resurrection of the body.

Webster 1828 Definition

Animate existence — underived in God, given to His creatures, brief and unpossessable in nature, and given again in Christ as spiritual and eternal life that begins in regeneration and ends in the resurrection of the body.

LIFE, n. plu. lives. 1. In a general sense, that state of animals and plants, or of an organized being, in which its natural functions and motions are performed, or in which its organs are capable of performing their functions.

2. In animals, animation; vitality; and in man, that state of being in which the soul and body are united.

3. The present state of existence; the time from birth to death. The life of man seldom exceeds seventy years.

4. Manner of living; conduct; deportment, in regard to morals. I will teach my family to lead good lives.

5. Eternal happiness in heaven; the spiritual state and endless felicity of the redeemed. This is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent. John 17. Also, the animating principle itself: Christ “who is our life” (Col 3:4).

Key Scripture

Gen 2:7 — "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul."

Joh 1:4 — "In him was life; and the life was the light of men."

Joh 10:10 — "The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly."

Jas 4:14 — "Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away."

Modern Corruption

Joh 10:10 has been detached from its shepherd-and-sheep setting and made the proof text of the prosperity gospel and of self-actualization — abundant life recast as health, wealth, and personal flourishing — while the culture severs the sanctity of life from its Giver and makes it a matter of quality and consent.

expand to see more

“Life more abundantly” is spoken in the middle of a discourse about a shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, and the very next verse says so. Wrenched out of it, the sentence has become the banner of the prosperity gospel — abundance as material increase and unbroken health — and of the softer self-actualization preaching that promises the listener his best life now. Both are refuted by the apostles' own lives, which were abundant in the sense John means and destitute in the sense the corruption means. The abundance in view is the quality of the life given: eternal, indestructible, life shared with the Son. Paul had it in a prison cell while writing about rejoicing.

The second corruption is the culture's. Where life is a possession rather than a trust, its worth is measured by projected quality and by the consent of the one holding it, and the weakest lose their claim first: the unborn, the disabled, the aged, the dying. The biblical ground is entirely different. Life is God's to give and God's to take, man is made in His image, and the shedding of innocent blood is therefore an offence against the Maker rather than a private calculation (Gen 9:6). The same doctrine that forbids the taking also commands the caring — the widow, the orphan, the stranger, the afflicted — and a church that defends the unborn while ignoring the aged has only half received it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chayyim (life, plural of abundance) and nephesh (living soul, breathing creature); Greek zōē (life as principle and gift), psychē (soul-life), and bios (the lived span and its means).

expand to see more

chayyim (Hebrew, H2416) — life; plural in form with singular agreement, a plural of fullness; it names the tree of life in Gen 2:9 and the book of life in Psa 69:28.

nephesh (Hebrew, H5315) — soul, living creature, breathing thing; Gen 2:7 says man became a living nephesh, so a man does not have a soul as one item among others but is one.

zōē (Greek, G2222) — life as principle and gift; John's word, occurring some thirty-six times in his Gospel, always of the life that is in the Son and given by Him.

psychē (Greek, G5590) — soul, the animating life; the word in Mat 16:25–26, where losing and saving the same psychē is the whole point of the paradox.

1689 London Baptist Confession 11.1 and 17.1 — justification and the perseverance of the saints; the confessional guarantee that the life given in regeneration cannot be finally lost, since it is Christ's life communicated and not the believer's achievement.

Usage

"Greek separates bios, psychē, and zōē where English has one word. Preachers reading Joh 10:10 should say plainly which is promised: it is zōē, and no promise about bios — the span or its means — is being made."

"James's vapour is not pessimism. It is the premise of an argument about presumption in business plans, and its conclusion is “ye ought to say, If the Lord will” — a doctrine of providence applied to a calendar."

"Because Gen 2:7 says man became a living soul rather than received one, the Hebrew resists any scheme that treats the body as a container the real person occupies temporarily — which is why the hope is resurrection rather than escape."
